Bidease, the New York mobile app advertising company, on October 23, 2026 named Dock Kim, a former Moloco revenue executive, as its Vice President of Business Development. Kim spent more than seven years at Moloco, one of the larger machine learning ad platforms for app marketers, and will lead Bidease's go-to-market work across North America, Latin America and EMEA. The appointment arrives with a set of growth claims from Bidease - revenue up more than 200 percent year over year in each of the past two years, and more than 650 million ad impressions served a day - none of which comes with an absolute figure attached.
In Short
A smaller company that buys ads inside mobile apps for app makers has hired a senior sales executive from Moloco, one of its much bigger rivals. The company says its revenue has more than tripled two years in a row, but it has not said how much money it actually makes, and its own website gives a smaller audience number than the announcement. For app marketers, it is one more sign that independent ad platforms are hiring people from the large players to compete for the same budgets.
The appointment
According to Bidease, Kim brings "nearly three decades" of industry experience. At Moloco he was, in the company's description, "at the helm" of go-to-market during the platform's main years of growth, first leading its revenue teams and later overseeing supply partnerships. His most recent title there was Global VP of Revenue & Sales, according to Bidease. The announcement does not give the date he left Moloco or the date he starts at Bidease.
The role is regional and commercial. Bidease says Kim will run go-to-market across North America, LATAM and EMEA "as it builds on that momentum in new and established markets." Two priorities are listed: growing revenue in North America, with named app categories including gaming, shopping and fintech, and accelerating global expansion, with specific mention of EMEA and emerging markets.
Boris Abaev, Bidease's chief executive, framed the hire around the company's technology and its pitch to buyers.
"Advanced machine learning with robust scale is central to how our campaigns perform, and Dock knows how to explain that to buyers in a way they can act on," Abaev said. "He's built revenue teams across regions at global scale, and that's exactly what we need for this stage of growth."
Kim's own statement describes Bidease as a demand-side platform, which is notable because the company's boilerplate calls itself a "performance advertising platform for mobile app growth" rather than a DSP.
"Marketers worldwide are looking for a DSP they can trust with growth - and Bidease is delivering, backed by smart talent and massive momentum," Kim said. "My job is to scale what's working and bring Bidease to more partners, especially in high-growth markets."
The growth claims
Bidease puts three numbers forward. Revenue grew by more than 200 percent year over year for each of the past two consecutive years. The platform serves more than 650 million ad impressions a day for advertisers worldwide. And the company has twice been named to the Financial Times' list of The Americas' Fastest-Growing Companies.
None of these is anchored to a base. Bidease is privately held and the announcement gives no revenue total, no fiscal-year boundaries for the two growth periods and no years for the FT list appearances. Growth above 200 percent means revenue more than tripled in each year; compounded over two years, that implies revenue at least nine times its level two years earlier, by PPC Land's own calculation. Without a starting figure, the multiple says little about absolute scale - a company tripling from a small base and one tripling from hundreds of millions of dollars would publish the same percentage.
Two impression figures
The 650 million figure also sits awkwardly beside Bidease's own website. The company's About Us page states that Bidease "has grown into a global leader in app marketing and monetization that delivers over 170 million ad impressions, daily." The same page describes "our 95-member team" working from headquarters in New York City and offices across the US, Europe and the Middle East.
The gap between 170 million and 650 million is nearly fourfold. The two numbers could reflect different periods, different counting methods or an About Us page that has not been updated; Bidease did not explain the difference in its announcement, and the release does not say how impressions are counted. The headcount figure of 95 is the only staff number either source gives.
There is a geographic gap as well. The appointment covers LATAM, yet the About Us page lists offices in the US, Europe and the Middle East only, and the release's boilerplate repeats that list. Its team page names a general manager for MENA, Shy Rahimi, and one for Eastern Europe, Gennadii Lurie, but no one with a Latin American remit.
What Bidease says it does
According to Bidease, the company was founded in 2016 and powers "user acquisition, re-engagement, and monetization for mobile apps across gaming, fintech, ecommerce, and beyond." The website menu breaks this into three products - User Acquisition, Re-Engagement and SDK - and three customer groups: marketers, publishers and agencies.
The monetization side matters for how the company should be read. A programmatic buying platform bids for inventory inside other companies' apps. Bidease also runs what the release calls "a growing SDK business," which places code inside publishers' apps and gives it a supply relationship alongside its buying business. The announcement offers no numbers for the SDK, such as the count of integrated apps or the share of revenue it brings in. Kim's last role at Moloco, overseeing supply partnerships, maps onto that side of the business.
The company describes its technology in general terms. The release refers to "predictive optimization and bidding intelligence," while the About Us page says Bidease works "with deep expertise and industry-leading neural networks" and promises "AI-powered campaigns." Neither page describes model architecture, training data, the signals used for bidding or how the company handles iOS users who have declined tracking. These are company self-descriptions, not independently tested claims.
The About Us page carries a separate statement from Abaev, credited there as co-founder and CEO: "In an industry that's often complex and opaque, we built Bidease to be different - fully transparent, performance-driven, and truly invested in our customers' success. When you work with us, you're not just getting a technology provider, you're getting a partner who cares."
The leadership bench
Kim joins an executive team that already has commercial seats filled. The Bidease team page lists Alex Kukuliev as co-founder and chief product officer, Ilia Varvaluk as chief technology officer, Boris Fourman as managing partner and chief revenue officer, Dennis Mink as chief marketing officer, Vadim Dyakov as chief financial officer, Michele Webb as head of sales for the Americas, Ross Barasch as VP partnerships, Sima Vance as global head of customer success and Diana Akhmetshin as general counsel. The release does not say whom Kim reports to, or how his go-to-market remit for North America divides with the existing head of sales for the Americas and the chief revenue officer.
Where Moloco stands
Kim's former employer has been busy on several fronts this year, and PPC Land's coverage shows a company extending well beyond its original mobile app buying business. In April, Moloco took its machine learning platform to connected TV with a Performance CTV product for app marketers, describing itself then as reaching two billion consumers across more than two million mobile apps. In June, it was one of four companies - with Google, Meta and Unity - that bought minority stakes in AppsFlyer at a $2.7 billion valuation, with neutrality terms barring preferential treatment in attribution. And earlier this month, Moloco became the first technology provider certified under IAB Europe's retail media programme, through its Commerce Media unit.
On performance rankings, the AppsFlyer Performance Index released in December 2025 kept Moloco fourth in its global power ranking for iOS gaming, behind larger networks.
That is the company Bidease is borrowing from. When the release calls Moloco "one of mobile's best-known ad platforms," it is also positioning Bidease as the smaller challenger hiring from a larger rival. Whether a revenue leader who built teams at Moloco's scale brings Moloco's buyer relationships with him is a separate question, and one the announcement does not address.
A crowded field for app budgets
The mobile app performance market Bidease is chasing has some very large incumbents. AppLovin reported $1.92 billion in second-quarter 2026 revenue, up 53 percent, with guidance of $2.06 billion to $2.09 billion for the third quarter. Liftoff, which merged with Vungle in 2021, went public on Nasdaq in June at $23 a share, disclosing 2025 revenue of $685.7 million and 649 full-time employees. The scale gap between those disclosed figures and a 95-person company is wide, which is why Bidease's undisclosed revenue base matters for anyone comparing its growth rate to theirs.
The competition is also turning litigious. In September, AppLovin filed for arbitration against Unity and sought a court order to stop data collection through Unity's Ad Quality SDK, a dispute that turns on what in-app code can see about competing bids. For a company like Bidease that runs both a buying platform and an SDK, those questions about supply-side access are not abstract.
Latin America has drawn other consolidation. In April, MiQ acquired Rocket Lab, a Miami-based mobile app growth company operating mainly in Latin America, whose website listed Moloco among its demand-side partners. Bidease's decision to put LATAM inside Kim's remit, without a named office there, places it in the same regional contest.
Why it matters for marketers
For app marketers allocating user acquisition budgets, a senior hire at a smaller DSP is a small data point, but it connects to a larger pattern PPC Land has tracked through 2026: the largest mobile ad platforms are consolidating, going public or moving into adjacent channels such as CTV and retail media, while smaller platforms compete on service and price in the mid-market. Bidease's own messaging leans on transparency and hands-on support, the same ground most challengers claim.
The measurable questions remain open. Buyers evaluating Bidease have a growth rate without a base, two daily impression figures nearly four times apart, a headcount of 95 and no published benchmark data. The company says Kim can explain its machine learning "in a way they can act on." The announcement itself does not yet do that.

Summary
Who: Bidease, a New York mobile app advertising company founded in 2016 and led by CEO Boris Abaev, and Dock Kim, who spent more than seven years at Moloco, most recently as Global VP of Revenue & Sales.
What: Bidease appointed Kim as Vice President of Business Development to lead go-to-market across North America, LATAM and EMEA. The company says its revenue grew more than 200 percent year over year in each of the past two years and that it serves more than 650 million ad impressions a day, though its About Us page states over 170 million and a 95-member team. No revenue totals were disclosed.
When: The appointment was announced on October 23, 2026.
Where: Bidease is headquartered in New York with offices in the US, Europe and the Middle East; Kim's remit covers North America, Latin America and EMEA.
Why: Bidease says it needs revenue leadership at global scale for its current growth stage, with priorities in North American gaming, shopping and fintech apps and in EMEA and emerging markets. The hire places a former executive from a larger rival inside a smaller platform competing for the same app marketing budgets.
